tasks.title: Passwordless SSH & secure file transfer
tasks.objective:
Host: workstation (as student)

Do this:
• Generate an SSH keypair on workstation (accept all defaults, no passphrase)
• Copy your public key to servera and serverb so you can SSH in with no password
• Copy /etc/hosts from workstation to /tmp/hosts.copy on servera
• Copy /etc/passwd from servera back to /tmp/passwd.copy on workstation

Done looks like: ssh student@servera true works with no password prompt, and both /tmp files exist with matching content.

tasks.title: File & directory management
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Build this exact layout:
/lab-test/
├── files/ → file1.txt containing exactly alpha
├── archive/ → file1.copy (copy of file1, contains alpha)
│                  → file2.moved (moved/renamed, contains beta)
└── extracted/ → empty directory

Key idea: file1 is copied (original stays), file2 is moved (original disappears), file3 is removed.

Done looks like: cat /lab-test/files/file1.txt prints "alpha", cat /lab-test/archive/file2.moved prints "beta".

tasks.title: Hard links and symbolic links
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Create a hard link /lab/files/file1.hard → /lab/files/file1.txt
• Create a symbolic link /lab/files/file1.soft → /lab/files/file1.txt (use the absolute path)

Key idea: A hard link shares the same inode (same data). A symlink is a pointer to a path.

Done looks like: ls -i shows file1.txt and file1.hard with the same inode number; readlink /lab/files/file1.soft prints the target path.

tasks.title: Directory permissions (760)
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Set /lab/files to mode 760 — that's rwx for owner, rw- for group, --- for others.

Done looks like: stat -c %a /lab/files prints 760.

tasks.title: stdout/stderr redirection
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student)

Do this: Run ls /root /notexist and split the output streams:
• Standard output → ~/stdout.log
• Standard error → ~/stderr.log

Key idea: 1> redirects stdout, 2> redirects stderr. They're separate streams.

Done looks like: stdout.log has the /root listing attempt, stderr.log has the "Permission denied" and "No such file" errors.

tasks.title: grep with regex to file
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student)

Do this: Search /etc/passwd for lines that start with a lowercase letter and contain "bash". Save matches to /tmp/bash-users.txt in original order.

Done looks like: cat /tmp/bash-users.txt shows matching user lines, each starting with a lowercase letter.

tasks.title: Create gzip tar archive
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Create a gzipped tar archive at /lab/archive/files.tar.gz containing the /lab/files directory.

Done looks like: tar -tzf /lab/archive/files.tar.gz lists the archived files including file1.txt.

tasks.title: Extract gzip tar archive
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Extract /lab/archive/files.tar.gz into /lab/extracted/ so that file1.txt is findable underneath with content alpha.

Done looks like: find /lab/extracted -name file1.txt -exec cat {} \; prints "alpha".

tasks.title: User and group management
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Create group developers
• Create user devuser with developers as primary group and wheel as supplementary group
• Set devuser's password to RedHat123
• Set maximum password age to 30 days

Done looks like: id devuser shows both groups; chage -l devuser shows "Maximum number of days: 30".

tasks.title: Sudoers drop-in for group
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Create /etc/sudoers.d/developers granting the developers group full sudo (%developers ALL=(ALL) ALL). Set mode 440. Never edit /etc/sudoers directly.

Done looks like: sudo visudo -c says "parsed OK"; stat -c %a /etc/sudoers.d/developers prints 440.

tasks.title: Shared directory with SGID and sticky bit
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Create /shared/dev owned by group developers with mode 3770:
• 3 = SGID (2) + sticky (1): new files inherit the group, only owners can delete
• 770 = rwx for owner and group, nothing for others

Done looks like: ls -ld /shared/dev shows drwxrws--T and group developers.

tasks.title: DNF repository configuration
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Create /etc/yum.repos.d/rocky.repo with exactly:
[rocky-baseos]
name=Rocky BaseOS
baseurl=https://dl.rockylinux.org/pub/rocky/9/BaseOS/x86_64/os/
enabled=1
gpgcheck=0

Done looks like: dnf repolist shows rocky-baseos.

tasks.title: Install htop with the package manager
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Install the EPEL repository (epel-release package)
• Install htop from EPEL

Done looks like: rpm -q htop shows the installed version.

tasks.title: GPT partitioning of the data disk
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: The unused data disk is /dev/sdb (~5 GB). Create a GPT partition table with:
• sdb1: 1 MiB → 2049 MiB (~2 GiB), type LVM
• sdb2: 2049 MiB → 2561 MiB (~512 MiB), type linux-swap

Warning: Writing a partition table is destructive — double-check you're on /dev/sdb.

Done looks like: lsblk /dev/sdb shows sdb1 (~2G) and sdb2 (~512M).

tasks.title: LVM: PV, VG vgdata, LV lvdata
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this (requires Q14's sdb1):
• Create a physical volume on /dev/sdb1
• Create volume group vgdata on it
• Create a 1 GiB logical volume named lvdata in vgdata

Done looks like: sudo lvs shows lvdata in vgdata, 1.00g.

tasks.title: XFS filesystem mounted at /data
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this (requires Q15's LV):
• Format /dev/vgdata/lvdata as XFS
• Mount it at /data

Done looks like: findmnt /data shows the mount with fstype xfs.

tasks.title: Swap on partition 2 with persistent fstab
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this (requires Q14's sdb2):
• Format /dev/sdb2 as swap and activate it now
• Add a persistent entry to /etc/fstab using the partition's UUID (not /dev/sdb2)
• Format: UUID=<uuid> swap swap defaults 0 0

Done looks like: swapon --show lists the swap; grep swap /etc/fstab shows the UUID entry.

tasks.title: Autofs NFS client mount
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Configure autofs so that serverb:/srv/nfs/share is automatically mounted at /nfs/share:
• Install autofs
• Add /nfs /etc/auto.nfs to /etc/auto.master
• Create /etc/auto.nfs with: share -rw,soft,intr serverb:/srv/nfs/share
• Enable and start autofs

Done looks like: ls /nfs/share/ triggers the mount and shows the shared files.

tasks.title: Background process with nice 15
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student)

Do this:
• Start sha1sum /dev/zero in the background (it burns CPU forever)
• Raise its nice value to 10, then to 15 (lower priority)

Key idea: Higher nice = nicer to other processes = lower priority.

Done looks like: ps -o pid,ni,comm -C sha1sum shows NI column = 15.

tasks.title: User-check shell script
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Create /root/checkuser.sh — a script that takes a username as $1 and prints exactly:
• User exists — if the user exists
• User does not exist — if not
Make it executable.

Done looks like: sudo /root/checkuser.sh root prints "User exists"; sudo /root/checkuser.sh nosuchuser prints "User does not exist".

tasks.title: Apache on 9092 with SELinux enforcing
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Install httpd (Apache)
• Create /webdata/html/index.html containing exactly It Works!!
• Make Apache listen on TCP port 9092
• SELinux: allow httpd to bind 9092 (http_port_t) and read /webdata/html (httpd_sys_content_t) — keep SELinux enforcing
• Enable and start httpd

Done looks like: curl -s http://localhost:9092/ prints "It Works!!".

tasks.title: firewalld permanent rules
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this (requires Q21):
• Open TCP port 9092 in the firewall permanently
• Allow the http service permanently
• Reload the firewall

Done looks like: firewall-cmd --list-ports --permanent shows 9092/tcp; --list-services --permanent shows http.

tasks.title: Default systemd target multi-user
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Set the default systemd target to multi-user.target (text console, no GUI).

Done looks like: systemctl get-default prints "multi-user.target".

tasks.title: SELinux runtime Permissive, boot Enforcing
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Set SELinux to Permissive right now (runtime, immediate)
• Configure SELinux to boot into Enforcing mode (persistent config)

Key idea: setenforce = now; /etc/selinux/config = after reboot.

Done looks like: getenforce prints "Permissive"; grep ^SELINUX= /etc/selinux/config shows "enforcing".

tasks.title: tuned throughput-performance
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Enable and start tuned
• Set the active profile to throughput-performance

Done looks like: tuned-adm active prints "throughput-performance".

tasks.title: Timezone Europe/Bucharest
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Set the system timezone to Europe/Bucharest.

Done looks like: timedatectl | grep Zone shows Europe/Bucharest.

tasks.title: Persistent systemd journal
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf
• Restart systemd-journald

Key idea: Persistent storage keeps logs in /var/log/journal across reboots.

Done looks like: ls -ld /var/log/journal shows the directory exists.

tasks.title: Capture sshd journal to file
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student)

Do this: Capture the full systemd journal for the sshd service into /tmp/sshd-logs.txt.

Done looks like: wc -l /tmp/sshd-logs.txt shows lines; the file is not empty.

tasks.title: NetworkManager static profile exam-conn
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Create a NetworkManager connection named exam-conn on interface docker0 with manual IPv4:
• Address: 192.168.56.200/24
• Gateway: 192.168.56.1
• DNS: 8.8.8.8

Done looks like: nmcli con show exam-conn shows all three values.

tasks.title: Append second address to exam-conn
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this (requires Q29): Add 192.168.56.210/24 as a second IPv4 address on exam-conn — without removing the existing .200 address.

Key idea: The + prefix appends; without it, nmcli replaces the value.

Done looks like: nmcli -g ipv4.addresses con show exam-conn shows both addresses.

tasks.title: Set system hostname
tasks.objective:
Host: servera (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Set the system hostname to servera.lab.example.com.

Done looks like: hostnamectl shows the new hostname.

tasks.title: Cron jobs (user + system)
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Create a cron job for user devuser that runs /usr/bin/true daily at 02:00
• Create a system-wide cron job in /etc/cron.d/ that runs /usr/bin/true as root every hour

Done looks like: crontab -u devuser -l shows the 02:00 entry; the /etc/cron.d file shows the hourly entry.

tasks.title: Flathub remote + VLC flatpak
tasks.objective:
Host: serverb (as student, use sudo)

Do this:
• Add the Flathub remote: https://flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
• Install VLC (org.videolan.VLC) from Flathub — this takes a few minutes

Done looks like: flatpak list shows org.videolan.VLC.

tasks.title: IPv4 packet forwarding (runtime)
tasks.objective:
Host: workstation (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Enable IPv4 packet forwarding at runtime (takes effect immediately, does not survive reboot).

Done looks like: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward prints "= 1".

tasks.title: IPv6 packet forwarding (runtime)
tasks.objective:
Host: workstation (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Enable IPv6 packet forwarding at runtime.

Done looks like: sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding prints "= 1".

tasks.title: Packet forwarding persistent (sysctl.d)
tasks.objective:
Host: workstation (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Make both IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding persistent across reboots by writing a /etc/sysctl.d/ drop-in file.

Key idea: Runtime sysctl -w is temporary; /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf is permanent.

Done looks like: The conf file contains both =1 lines; sysctl shows both as 1.

tasks.title: Remove rhgb/quiet kernel args
tasks.objective:
Host: workstation (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Remove the quiet and splash kernel arguments from all installed kernels (so boot messages are visible).

Done looks like: grubby --info=ALL shows no kernel with "quiet" or "splash" in its args.

tasks.title: Find large files report
tasks.objective:
Host: workstation (as student, use sudo)

Do this: Find all files on the system that are bigger than 200 MB but smaller than 500 MB. Save their full paths to /root/large-files-report.txt. Suppress permission-denied noise.

Done looks like: cat /root/large-files-report.txt lists matching file paths, one per line.

Q01.title: Passwordless SSH & secure file transfer
Q01.why: Remote administration fails when authentication, hostname resolution or transfer direction is misunderstood. This lab tests key trust and exact copies between hosts, so a successful interactive login alone is insufficient.

concepts.title: Hosts and sessions
concepts.explanation: A host is a separate computer with its own files and users. Open the portal terminal on workstation; all commands below execute there. An interactive ssh opens a remote shell until exit. Commands chained after that interactive session execute back on the source after logout.

concepts.title: Key authentication
concepts.explanation: SSH encrypts a session and checks the server identity using a host key. Your user keypair is different: the private key stays on workstation; the public key is added to the destination user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The server verifies a signature without receiving the private key. A key passphrase protects the private key locally; a server password authenticates the account remotely.

concepts.title: Transfer direction
concepts.explanation: scp takes source then destination. A colon separates a remote host from its path; an unqualified path belongs to the machine running scp. /etc/passwd lists accounts, not their password hashes. diff compares file contents and returns zero for identical files.

variations.title: Reverse transfer
variations.objective: Copy serverb:/etc/hosts into ~/hosts.serverb on workstation and compare it with a remote read.
variations.success: The local file is byte-identical; the source remains on serverb.

variations.title: Select a key

exam_traps: Passwordless SSH is per user and destination; testing from the controller does not prove workstation trust.
Never copy the private key to authorized_keys.
Do not disable host-key checking to conceal an unexpected server identity; verify it.

troubleshooting.cause: Name resolution failed before authentication.
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect getent hosts servera and the workstation /etc/hosts entry.

troubleshooting.cause: Wrong identity, account, trust file or restrictive permissions.
troubleshooting.fix: Use ssh -v student@servera; verify ~/.ssh is 700 and authorized_keys is 600 on the destination.

troubleshooting.cause: Known host identity differs, possibly after a fixture rebuild.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the expected VM fingerprint with the operator before updating the known_hosts entry.

self_check.question: Which key is copied to the server?
self_check.answer: Only the public key; the private key stays on the source.

self_check.question: Where does scp’s unqualified destination live?
self_check.answer: On the machine running scp.

self_check.question: Why use BatchMode=yes?
self_check.answer: It prevents a password prompt from masking failed key authentication.

deeper.title: Automation
deeper.explanation: Use explicit identity files, verified host keys and timeouts in scripts. Agent forwarding delegates use of a key and should be limited to trusted hosts.

deeper.title: Connections
deeper.explanation: Q02 handles local copy semantics; Q28 inspects sshd logs when an authentication request reaches the server but fails.

man_page_research.intro: Start by identifying the system concept in the objective, then use the manuals below to discover syntax and constraints yourself. Search inside a man page by typing / followed by the shown text, then press n for the next match.

steps.clue: Identify how to choose a key type and where keys are written.

Q03.title: Hard links and symbolic links
Q03.why: Links let multiple names refer to data without blindly duplicating it. The exam distinguishes a shared inode from a path pointer and may deliberately move or delete the original.

concepts.title: Inodes
concepts.explanation: A filesystem inode records metadata and data locations. A directory entry gives it a name. Two hard links name the same inode and share content; deleting one name leaves the inode while another name or open descriptor references it.

concepts.title: Symbolic links
concepts.explanation: A symlink is a separate inode containing a target path. Access follows that path, so a removed target leaves a dangling link. Relative targets are resolved from the symlink’s directory, not your current directory.

concepts.title: Limits
concepts.explanation: Ordinary users cannot hard-link directories, and hard links cannot cross filesystems. Symlinks can point across filesystems or to nonexistent targets.

Q04.title: Directory permissions (760)
Q04.why: Directory permissions decide whether someone can discover names, traverse paths or modify entries. Exam modes must be exact even when a deliberately unusual mode is unsuitable for normal shared-directory use.

concepts.title: Permission classes
concepts.explanation: Linux first chooses owner, then matching group, then other. It does not add the three classes together. Read=4, write=2 and execute=1 produce octal digits: 7 is all three; 6 is read plus write; 0 is none.

concepts.title: Directory meanings
concepts.explanation: For directories, read lists names, execute permits search/traversal and access to named children, and write changes directory entries when search is also allowed. Group rw without x in mode 760 does not provide useful normal child access.

concepts.title: Beyond mode bits
concepts.explanation: Owner and group identities determine which class applies. ACLs can add named entries and a mask limiting effective rights. SELinux can deny access even when ordinary permissions allow it.

concepts.title: Directory ownership

concepts.title: SGID

concepts.title: Sticky

Q14.title: GPT partitioning of the data disk
Q14.why: A partitioning mistake can destroy the operating system rather than prepare extra storage. This task tests GPT layout, binary size boundaries and an LVM partition flag on the dedicated /dev/sdb lab data disk.

concepts.title: Disk versus partition
concepts.explanation: A disk is a block device, such as /dev/sdb; its partitions are bounded regions, such as /dev/sdb1. A partition table describes regions. GPT is a modern table format; a filesystem or LVM physical volume comes later.

concepts.title: Units and alignment
concepts.explanation: MiB is 2^20 bytes and GiB is 2^30 bytes. Starting at 1 MiB avoids the table and gives conventional alignment. A region from 1 to 2049 MiB spans 2048 MiB = 2 GiB. 2049 to 2561 spans 512 MiB.

concepts.title: Layering
concepts.explanation: The LVM flag marks intended partition use but does not create a physical volume. A linux-swap partition type does not initialize swap data. Q15 and Q17 perform those distinct operations.

concepts.title: Virtual memory

concepts.title: Initialization and identity

concepts.title: fstab fields

concepts.title: Processes

concepts.title: Nice values
concepts.explanation: For normal scheduling, nice ranges from -20 (higher priority) to 19 (lower priority); larger numbers are nicer to competitors. Q20.title: User-check shell script
Q20.why: Small administrative scripts must report truthful results without leaking diagnostic noise. The exam checks exact messages, argument handling and executable permission, so pretty-looking source alone is insufficient.

concepts.title: Arguments
concepts.explanation: The shell passes words to a script. $1 is the first positional argument; double quotes preserve it as a single value even when empty or containing spaces. The shebang selects the interpreter when the file is executed directly.

concepts.title: Exit status
concepts.explanation: A program returns zero for success and nonzero for failure. if runs a command and branches on that status. id USER queries the configured account database; unlike a grep substring it checks an actual identity.

concepts.title: Here-document
concepts.explanation: A quoted EOF delimiter prevents the outer shell expanding $1 while writing the script. Otherwise the stored file could contain the current terminal’s argument rather than the script’s future argument.

commands.command:
sudo tee /root/checkuser.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
if id "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  printf 'User exists\n'
else
  printf 'User does not exist\n'
fi
EOF
commands.why: Write literal script source; id’s status supplies the decision and both output streams are hidden.

Q21.title: Apache on 9092 with SELinux enforcing
Q21.why: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.

concepts.title: Web serving
concepts.explanation: Apache maps HTTP requests to its configured DocumentRoot. Listen opens a TCP port; it does not change the document root. A Directory block authorizes access to a custom filesystem path. Syntax must be valid before restart.

concepts.title: SELinux types
concepts.explanation: Enforcing policy checks the httpd process against port and file types. http_port_t permits Apache’s network bind; httpd_sys_content_t permits reading static content. Ordinary 755/644 permissions still matter independently.

concepts.title: Persistent labels
concepts.explanation: semanage fcontext adds a path-to-type rule; restorecon applies that rule to existing files. chcon changes current labels but can be lost after relabeling. Port policy is separate from firewalld network filtering.

Q22.title: firewalld permanent rules
Q22.why: A service can work locally while a firewall blocks every client. The exercise tests permanent rules and their loaded runtime state, requiring the correct zone and protocol.

concepts.title: Firewalld
concepts.explanation: Firewalld groups rules into zones assigned to interfaces/sources. The default zone is used when no zone is specified, but the active interface may use a different zone. Inspect active zones before modifying policy.

concepts.title: Two configurations

concepts.explanation: Throughput is work completed per time interval; latency is delay experienced by one operation. Optimizing one can worsen the other. A profile is a predefined collection of kernel/power/resource settings, not a universal speed button.

Q26.title: Timezone Europe/Bucharest
Q26.why: The wrong timezone makes schedules and event timelines confusing even when the system clock is correct. The exam checks the named timezone, not a manually adjusted wall clock.

concepts.title: Clock and zone
concepts.explanation: A system clock represents time; a timezone maps that time to local civil time, including daylight-saving rules. Changing timezone changes display and scheduling interpretation without necessarily changing the underlying instant.

concepts.title: Names
concepts.explanation: Europe/Bucharest is an IANA zone name backed by installed timezone data. Fixed abbreviations are ambiguous and do not capture the complete daylight-saving/history rules.

concepts.title: NTP distinction
concepts.explanation: Time synchronization corrects clock drift. Setting a zone does not enable NTP or prove the clock is accurate. Cron in Q32 normally interprets schedule fields in the host’s configured timezone.

Q36.title: Packet forwarding persistent (sysctl.d)
Q36.why: Runtime settings vanish unless the boot configuration reapplies them. The exercise joins both protocol families in a persistent drop-in and verifies that intended settings also reached the running kernel.

concepts.title: sysctl.d
concepts.explanation: Files ending .conf in sysctl.d provide key=value assignments loaded by system startup tooling. A dedicated /etc/sysctl.d file is easier to maintain than replacing a shared configuration wholesale.

concepts.title: Ordering
concepts.explanation: Configuration files are ordered by name and may be overridden by later assignments or other services. A high-numbered filename is a convention, not proof that nothing else overrides it. Read runtime values after applying.

concepts.title: Two kinds of proof

Q38.why: Large-file reports must contain real paths rather than permission errors or directories. The exam checks both completeness and size limits, requiring understanding of find’s predicate logic and rounded size units.

concepts.title: Traversal
concepts.explanation: find recursively walks from each starting path. / includes multiple mounted filesystems unless restricted. -type f selects regular files; directories, sockets and symlinks are different types under the default non-following behavior.

concepts.title: Predicate logic
concepts.explanation: Adjacent tests are implicitly ANDed. -size +200M selects sizes rounded up to MiB that exceed 200; -size -500M selects rounded-up MiB strictly below 500. M means 1,048,576 bytes, not decimal megabytes.

concepts.title: Boundary subtlety
concepts.explanation: The legacy grader’s expected traversal uses +200M -500M, so this lesson follows it. Because GNU find rounds up to units, -500M excludes a portion of the byte interval below exactly 500 MiB. A strict-byte variation uses c units with explicit byte thresholds; learn the distinction instead of claiming the two expressions are identical.

Q01.why: Remote administration fails when authentication, hostname resolution or transfer direction is misunderstood. This lab tests key trust and exact copies between hosts, so a successful interactive login alone is insufficient.

deeper_why.title: Hosts and sessions
deeper_why.explanation: A host is a separate computer with its own files and users. Open the portal terminal on workstation; all commands below execute there. An interactive ssh opens a remote shell until exit. Commands chained after that interactive session execute back on the source after logout.

deeper_why.title: Key authentication
deeper_why.explanation: SSH encrypts a session and checks the server identity using a host key. Your user keypair is different: the private key stays on workstation; the public key is added to the destination user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The server verifies a signature without receiving the private key. A key passphrase protects the private key locally; a server password authenticates the account remotely.

deeper_why.title: Transfer direction
deeper_why.explanation: scp takes source then destination. A colon separates a remote host from its path; an unqualified path belongs to the machine running scp. /etc/passwd lists accounts, not their password hashes. diff compares file contents and returns zero for identical files.

misconceptions.observable: The answer starts with a utility unrelated to the requested operation.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may focus on a familiar tool instead of the object the task asks to change.
misconceptions.explanation: Choose a utility based on the operation: query, create, modify, activate, persist, or verify.
misconceptions.micro: Name the object and the operation first. Then choose the utility that owns that configuration. For example, DNF installs packages while rpm -q only checks the local database. Retry by naming the state that must change and the command family responsible.
misconceptions.consequence: The requested state is not changed even if the command succeeds.
misconceptions.retry: Select the tool that performs the requested change, then name the separate verification tool.
misconceptions.man: Use apropos <topic> and inspect the specific command man page.

misconceptions.observable: A required operand or value is missing.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may treat an option as self-contained when it expects a following value.
misconceptions.explanation: Many flags consume a value such as a group name, protocol, path, or unit.
misconceptions.micro: Read the synopsis and check which options take a following argument. A missing value can make the next token be interpreted as the option value. Retry by pairing each value-taking option with its operand.
misconceptions.consequence: The command fails or applies a value to the wrong token.
misconceptions.retry: Set a 45-day maximum password age for devuser, including its numeric value.
misconceptions.man: Open the command’s man page and search for the option.

misconceptions.observable: The utility and option shape match, but a path, name, address, size, or other value differs from the objective.
misconceptions.likely: The command may target a nearby but different object or configuration value.
misconceptions.explanation: Linux utilities act on the operands and values you supply. A syntactically valid command can succeed while changing or checking the wrong target.
misconceptions.micro: Before running a state-changing command, compare every pathname, account, device, service, address, and numeric value with the objective. Two valid commands can have the same flags yet affect different objects. For example, `chmod 750 /srv/site` and `chmod 750 /srv/sites` are both valid, but only one may be the requested directory. Recheck the exact target and verify the resulting state. Retry by inspecting a known harmless path.
misconceptions.consequence: The command can succeed against the wrong resource while the required resource remains unchanged.
misconceptions.retry: Inspect a known path exactly, then compare its name with the requested target.
misconceptions.man: man path/to/command; inspect the OPERANDS section.

misconceptions.observable: The remote and local operands are reversed.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may assume scp uses destination-first order.
misconceptions.explanation: scp uses source first and destination second. A host:path operand marks the remote side.
misconceptions.micro: Read an scp command from left to right: source, then destination. A local path has no host prefix; a remote path uses user@host:path. Reversing the operands copies in the opposite direction, which can overwrite or create a file on the wrong machine. Retry by copying a local file to a new remote filename.
misconceptions.consequence: The bytes travel in the opposite direction from the objective.

misconceptions.man: man scp; search for SOURCE and DESTINATION.

Q02.why: Incorrect copy, move or delete choices can lose the only version of a file. The exam checks the final tree and exact contents, including paths that must disappear.

deeper_why.title: Paths
deeper_why.explanation: An absolute path begins with /; a relative path starts at the current working directory. A directory maps names to files. mkdir makes directories, cp duplicates data, mv relocates a name, and rm unlinks it.

deeper_why.title: Shell expansion
deeper_why.explanation: Bash expands {files,archive,extracted} into three arguments before mkdir starts. Quotes preserve literal text. tee writes as root when preceded by sudo; sudo echo with a user-owned redirection does not.

deeper_why.title: Copy versus move
deeper_why.explanation: A copy leaves the source intact. A move within one filesystem usually renames a directory entry; a move across filesystems copies then removes. Removing a path is not a recycle-bin operation.

Q03.why: Links let multiple names refer to data without blindly duplicating it. The exam distinguishes a shared inode from a path pointer and may deliberately move or delete the original.

deeper_why.title: Inodes
deeper_why.explanation: A filesystem inode records metadata and data locations. A directory entry gives it a name. Two hard links name the same inode and share content; deleting one name leaves the inode while another name or open descriptor references it.

deeper_why.title: Symbolic links
deeper_why.explanation: A symlink is a separate inode containing a target path. Access follows that path, so a removed target leaves a dangling link. Relative targets are resolved from the symlink’s directory, not your current directory.

deeper_why.title: Limits
deeper_why.explanation: Ordinary users cannot hard-link directories, and hard links cannot cross filesystems. Symlinks can point across filesystems or to nonexistent targets.

Q04.why: Directory permissions decide whether someone can discover names, traverse paths or modify entries. Exam modes must be exact even when a deliberately unusual mode is unsuitable for normal shared-directory use.

deeper_why.title: Permission classes
deeper_why.explanation: Linux first chooses owner, then matching group, then other. It does not add the three classes together. Read=4, write=2 and execute=1 produce octal digits: 7 is all three; 6 is read plus write; 0 is none.

deeper_why.title: Directory meanings
deeper_why.explanation: For directories, read lists names, execute permits search/traversal and access to named children, and write changes directory entries when search is also allowed. Group rw without x in mode 760 does not provide useful normal child access.

deeper_why.title: Beyond mode bits
deeper_why.explanation: Owner and group identities determine which class applies. ACLs can add named entries and a mask limiting effective rights. SELinux can deny access even when ordinary permissions allow it.

deeper_why.title: Processes
deeper_why.explanation: A running program has a process ID (PID). Shell job numbers identify jobs only within that shell; a PID is the kernel identifier used by renice and kill. The background operator & lets the shell continue without waiting.

deeper_why.title: Nice values
deeper_why.explanation: For normal scheduling, nice ranges from -20 (higher priority) to 19 (lower priority); larger numbers are nicer to competitors. deeper_why.explanation: /dev/zero produces endless zero bytes. sha1sum cannot finish reading it, so it consumes CPU and is intentionally left running for grading. Redirections discard output and errors; avoid launching multiple burners accidentally.

Q20.why: Small administrative scripts must report truthful results without leaking diagnostic noise. The exam checks exact messages, argument handling and executable permission, so pretty-looking source alone is insufficient.

deeper_why.title: Arguments
deeper_why.explanation: The shell passes words to a script. $1 is the first positional argument; double quotes preserve it as a single value even when empty or containing spaces. The shebang selects the interpreter when the file is executed directly.

deeper_why.title: Exit status
deeper_why.explanation: A program returns zero for success and nonzero for failure. if runs a command and branches on that status. id USER queries the configured account database; unlike a grep substring it checks an actual identity.

deeper_why.title: Here-document
deeper_why.explanation: A quoted EOF delimiter prevents the outer shell expanding $1 while writing the script. Otherwise the stored file could contain the current terminal’s argument rather than the script’s future argument.

commands.command:
sudo tee /root/checkuser.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
if id "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  printf 'User exists\n'
else
  printf 'User does not exist\n'
fi
EOF
commands.purpose: Write literal script source; id’s status supplies the decision and both output streams are hidden.

parts.effect: Only the following program receives root privileges; shell redirection still belongs to your current shell.
parts.without: Protected writes and administrative changes usually fail with permission denied.
parts.danger: Root bypasses ordinary file permissions. Check host and target before modifying anything.

parts.meaning: Copy standard input to a file and standard output

misconceptions.observable: The command is assigned to a host other than the lesson’s target.

misconceptions.observable: The answer starts with a utility unrelated to the requested operation.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may focus on a familiar tool instead of the object the task asks to change.
misconceptions.explanation: Choose a utility based on the operation: query, create, modify, activate, persist, or verify.
misconceptions.micro: Name the object and the operation first. Then choose the utility that owns that configuration. For example, DNF installs packages while rpm -q only checks the local database. Retry by naming the state that must change and the command family responsible.
misconceptions.consequence: The requested state is not changed even if the command succeeds.
misconceptions.retry: Select the tool that performs the requested change, then name the separate verification tool.
misconceptions.man: Use apropos <topic> and inspect the specific command man page.

misconceptions.observable: A required operand or value is missing.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may treat an option as self-contained when it expects a following value.
misconceptions.explanation: Many flags consume a value such as a group name, protocol, path, or unit.
misconceptions.micro: Read the synopsis and check which options take a following argument. A missing value can make the next token be interpreted as the option value. Retry by pairing each value-taking option with its operand.
misconceptions.consequence: The command fails or applies a value to the wrong token.
misconceptions.retry: Set a 45-day maximum password age for devuser, including its numeric value.
misconceptions.man: Open the command’s man page and search for the option.

misconceptions.observable: The utility and option shape match, but a path, name, address, size, or other value differs from the objective.
misconceptions.likely: The command may target a nearby but different object or configuration value.
misconceptions.explanation: Linux utilities act on the operands and values you supply. A syntactically valid command can succeed while changing or checking the wrong target.
misconceptions.micro: Before running a state-changing command, compare every pathname, account, device, service, address, and numeric value with the objective. Two valid commands can have the same flags yet affect different objects. For example, `chmod 750 /srv/site` and `chmod 750 /srv/sites` are both valid, but only one may be the requested directory. Recheck the exact target and verify the resulting state. Retry by inspecting a known harmless path.
misconceptions.consequence: The command can succeed against the wrong resource while the required resource remains unchanged.
misconceptions.retry: Inspect a known path exactly, then compare its name with the requested target.
misconceptions.man: man path/to/command; inspect the OPERANDS section.

misconceptions.observable: Output and error streams are sent to the wrong destinations or combined in the wrong order.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may treat file descriptors as interchangeable or redirections as order-independent.
misconceptions.explanation: 1 is stdout, 2 is stderr. Redirections are processed left to right; 2>&1 copies stdout’s current destination at that point.
misconceptions.micro: Shell redirection changes where each file descriptor points. In cmd >out 2>&1, stderr follows stdout into out. In cmd 2>&1 >out, stderr keeps the original stdout destination. Use separate 1> and 2> targets when the task requires separate files. Retry with harmless output in a temporary directory.
misconceptions.consequence: Diagnostics can be lost in the wrong file or mixed into a report.
misconceptions.retry: Route stdout to out.txt and stderr to err.txt.
misconceptions.man: man bash; search for “Redirections”.

Q21.why: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.

deeper_why.title: Web serving
deeper_why.explanation: Apache maps HTTP requests to its configured DocumentRoot. Listen opens a TCP port; it does not change the document root. A Directory block authorizes access to a custom filesystem path. Syntax must be valid before restart.

deeper_why.title: SELinux types
deeper_why.explanation: Enforcing policy checks the httpd process against port and file types. http_port_t permits Apache’s network bind; httpd_sys_content_t permits reading static content. Ordinary 755/644 permissions still matter independently.

deeper_why.title: Persistent labels
deeper_why.explanation: semanage fcontext adds a path-to-type rule; restorecon applies that rule to existing files. chcon changes current labels but can be lost after relabeling. Port policy is separate from firewalld network filtering.

comparisons.title: SELinux port type versus file type
comparisons.objective: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.
comparisons.question: Which persistent rule allows Apache to bind to TCP 9092?
comparisons.explanation: The port rule labels a TCP port with http_port_t. The fcontext rule maps filesystem paths to file types. They solve independent SELinux checks.
comparisons.verify: Use semanage port -l and semanage fcontext -l -C to inspect the persistent rules.

comparisons.title: fcontext rule versus restorecon
comparisons.objective: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.
comparisons.question: Which command applies the default label recorded by SELinux policy to existing files?
comparisons.explanation: semanage fcontext records a persistent path rule. restorecon applies the policy’s expected context to existing filesystem objects.
comparisons.verify: Use ls -Zd on the directory and index file after restorecon.

comparisons.title: Service enabled versus started
comparisons.objective: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.
comparisons.question: Which operation both enables a service for boot and starts it now?
comparisons.explanation: enable configures future startup; --now also starts the unit in the current boot. Neither proves that firewall access or SELinux policy is correct.
comparisons.verify: Use systemctl is-enabled, systemctl is-active, and curl to verify separate layers.

comparisons.title: Restart versus reload
comparisons.objective: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.
comparisons.question: Which action requests re-reading configuration without a full stop/start when the unit supports reload?
comparisons.explanation: reload asks the service to apply configuration through its reload action; restart stops and starts the service. Not every unit supports reload, so check CanReload and the service documentation first.
comparisons.verify: Use systemctl show -p CanReload httpd and inspect service status afterward.

misconceptions.explanation: Many flags consume a value such as a group name, protocol, path, or unit.
misconceptions.micro: Read the synopsis and check which options take a following argument. A missing value can make the next token be interpreted as the option value. Retry by pairing each value-taking option with its operand.
misconceptions.consequence: The command fails or applies a value to the wrong token.
misconceptions.retry: Set a 45-day maximum password age for devuser, including its numeric value.
misconceptions.man: Open the command’s man page and search for the option.

misconceptions.observable: The utility and option shape match, but a path, name, address, size, or other value differs from the objective.
misconceptions.likely: The command may target a nearby but different object or configuration value.
misconceptions.explanation: Linux utilities act on the operands and values you supply. A syntactically valid command can succeed while changing or checking the wrong target.
misconceptions.micro: Before running a state-changing command, compare every pathname, account, device, service, address, and numeric value with the objective. Two valid commands can have the same flags yet affect different objects. For example, `chmod 750 /srv/site` and `chmod 750 /srv/sites` are both valid, but only one may be the requested directory. Recheck the exact target and verify the resulting state. Retry by inspecting a known harmless path.
misconceptions.consequence: The command can succeed against the wrong resource while the required resource remains unchanged.
misconceptions.retry: Inspect a known path exactly, then compare its name with the requested target.
misconceptions.man: man path/to/command; inspect the OPERANDS section.

misconceptions.observable: The protocol selector is confused with a directory option.
misconceptions.likely: The same flag spelling may be generalized across unrelated utilities.
misconceptions.explanation: For semanage port, -p specifies the protocol (tcp or udp). For mkdir, -p creates parent directories.
misconceptions.micro: A short option has meaning only in its command context. In semanage port -p tcp, -p introduces the network protocol. In mkdir -p, it creates missing parent directories. Do not transfer a flag definition between utilities. Retry by labeling a safe test TCP port.
misconceptions.consequence: SELinux may not receive the intended protocol-qualified port rule.
misconceptions.retry: Label TCP port 9093 as an HTTP port using semanage port.
misconceptions.man: man semanage-port; man mkdir.

misconceptions.observable: A persistent file-context rule is missing or existing files are not relabeled.
misconceptions.likely: The answer may treat rule creation and applying the rule as one action.
misconceptions.explanation: semanage fcontext records a persistent mapping; restorecon applies the expected label to existing paths.
misconceptions.micro: SELinux file contexts have a stored policy mapping and labels on actual inodes. Add a persistent mapping with semanage fcontext, then run restorecon to apply it. Doing only one leaves either future relabeling or current files incorrect. Retry with a separate scratch path.
misconceptions.correct_example: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/webdata/html(/.*)?' followed by restorecon -Rv /webdata/html
misconceptions.consequence: Unix permissions may allow access while SELinux still blocks it, or a temporary label may revert.
misconceptions.retry: Create and apply a persistent content label rule for /srv/site.
misconceptions.man: man semanage-fcontext; man restorecon.

capstone.preconditions: On serverb, SELinux must be enforcing, httpd and SELinux management tools must be available, and the intended document root must be safe to create.

reference_solution.command:
sudo tee /etc/httpd/conf.d/lab9092.conf <<'EOF'
Listen 9092
<VirtualHost *:9092>
  DocumentRoot /webdata/html
  <Directory /webdata/html>
    Require all granted
  </Directory>
</VirtualHost>
EOF

Q22.why: A service can work locally while a firewall blocks every client. The exercise tests permanent rules and their loaded runtime state, requiring the correct zone and protocol.

deeper_why.title: Firewalld
deeper_why.explanation: Firewalld groups rules into zones assigned to interfaces/sources. The default zone is used when no zone is specified, but the active interface may use a different zone. Inspect active zones before modifying policy.

deeper_why.title: Two configurations
deeper_why.explanation: Runtime rules affect packets now; permanent rules are stored for reload/start. --permanent changes only stored policy. --reload replaces runtime policy with permanent policy and can drop runtime-only changes.

deeper_why.title: Port and service
deeper_why.explanation: 9092/tcp is an explicit transport port. The http service usually opens TCP 80, not the custom 9092 port. Both are requested, so one cannot substitute for the other.

deeper_why.explanation: systemd manages units representing services, mounts, sockets and more. A target groups dependencies and synchronization points; it is not a single daemon. multi-user.target supplies normal nongraphical multiuser operation.

deeper_why.title: Default versus current
deeper_why.explanation: set-default changes the default.target link used by future boots. It does not immediately switch the running system. isolate switches active units now and can stop services or your current session.

deeper_why.title: GUI dependency
deeper_why.explanation: graphical.target builds on multi-user services and adds graphical login components. Being connected through SSH does not reveal the configured default target.

Q24.why: Runtime troubleshooting and future security posture are separate decisions. This exercise deliberately requests permissive now and enforcing after boot, so making both states the same would fail the contract.

deeper_why.title: Enforcement
deeper_why.explanation: SELinux enforcing blocks policy-disallowed operations and records denials. Permissive records many would-be denials without enforcing them. Disabled is different: the enforcement system is not active, and setenforce cannot enable it.

deeper_why.title: Runtime change
deeper_why.explanation: setenforce controls the loaded policy’s current enforcement mode. It does not edit /etc/selinux/config. Root privileges are required to change mode.

deeper_why.title: Boot change
deeper_why.explanation: SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config controls intended future mode; kernel boot overrides can affect actual boot behavior. This task checks both current mode and persistent config text, without authorizing a VM reboot from the portal.

deeper_why.title: Tuning
deeper_why.explanation: Throughput is work completed per time interval; latency is delay experienced by one operation. Optimizing one can worsen the other. A profile is a predefined collection of kernel/power/resource settings, not a universal speed button.

deeper_why.title: Daemon and client

deeper_why.title: Persistence
deeper_why.explanation: Selecting a profile records tuned’s choice, but the daemon must run and be enabled for reliable boot application. Runtime sysctl commands elsewhere may conflict with a tuning profile managing the same setting.

Q26.why: The wrong timezone makes schedules and event timelines confusing even when the system clock is correct. The exam checks the named timezone, not a manually adjusted wall clock.

deeper_why.title: Clock and zone
deeper_why.explanation: A system clock represents time; a timezone maps that time to local civil time, including daylight-saving rules. Changing timezone changes display and scheduling interpretation without necessarily changing the underlying instant.

deeper_why.title: Names
deeper_why.explanation: Europe/Bucharest is an IANA zone name backed by installed timezone data. Fixed abbreviations are ambiguous and do not capture the complete daylight-saving/history rules.

deeper_why.title: NTP distinction
deeper_why.explanation: Time synchronization corrects clock drift. Setting a zone does not enable NTP or prove the clock is accurate. Cron in Q32 normally interprets schedule fields in the host’s configured timezone.

Q27.why: Volatile logs disappear after reboot, removing the evidence needed to explain failures. This task establishes persistent journald storage and applies the configuration while preserving other settings.

deeper_why.title: Journal
deeper_why.explanation: systemd-journald collects structured logs from services, kernel and other sources. Its binary journal supports queries by unit, boot, priority and time; it is not just one plain-text log file.

deeper_why.title: Storage modes
deeper_why.explanation: volatile writes under /run/log/journal, which is temporary. persistent writes under /var/log/journal when writable, with early-boot fallback. auto uses persistent storage when the appropriate directory exists. none drops stored logs while forwarding may still be configured.

deeper_why.title: Configuration precedence
deeper_why.explanation: The main file has a [Journal] section; drop-ins can override it. A file change does not automatically reconfigure a running daemon. This task’s grader checks the main Storage=persistent line and directory existence, but robust evidence includes a flush and later boot queries.

deeper_why.explanation: A device is a live kernel interface. A NetworkManager connection profile stores intended settings and may be inactive. One device can have multiple profiles, and connection names are not interface names.

deeper_why.title: IPv4 basics
deeper_why.explanation: 192.168.56.200/24 combines address with a 24-bit network prefix. The gateway is a next-hop router, not the local address. DNS translates names; it does not route packets. manual means address settings are provided explicitly rather than through DHCP.

deeper_why.title: Hostname
deeper_why.explanation: A fully qualified domain name combines host label and domain, here servera.lab.example.com. Linux’s configured hostname is local identity; DNS is a separate mapping service.

deeper_why.title: Static and transient
deeper_why.explanation: systemd distinguishes static, transient and pretty hostnames. A static hostname is stored for persistence; a transient one may come from network configuration. The ordinary set-hostname operation sets the practical system hostname fields.

deeper_why.title: Resolution
deeper_why.explanation: Changing hostname does not update every client’s /etc/hosts or DNS zone. SSH targets can still resolve through fixture aliases even after local machine identity changes.

Q32.why: A schedule can look plausible yet never run because its grammar, user context or daemon is wrong. The exercise checks a user’s daily 02:00 job and a separate hourly root job in /etc/cron.d.

deeper_why.title: Five fields
deeper_why.explanation: Cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, then command. 0 2 * * * means every day at 02:00; 0 * * * * means minute zero of every hour. It is not every minute.

deeper_why.title: Two formats
deeper_why.explanation: A user crontab runs as that user and has no username column. /etc/cron.d uses the same five time fields plus a username before the command. Mixing formats makes a job invalid or executes the wrong text.

deeper_why.title: Environment
deeper_why.explanation: Cron has a minimal environment and the system’s scheduling timezone, affected by daylight-saving behavior. Use absolute program paths. The original mock uses /usr/bin/true as a harmless demonstration, not a substantive maintenance job.

comparisons.objective: A schedule can look plausible yet never run because its grammar, user context or daemon is wrong. The exercise checks a user’s daily 02:00 job and a separate hourly root job in /etc/cron.d.

Q33.why: Desktop application packaging uses its own remote, runtime and installation scope, separate from RPM. This legacy mock task covers Flatpak/VLC; it is not a Podman container exercise and should not be represented as complete current EX200 coverage.

deeper_why.title: Flatpak
deeper_why.explanation: Flatpak installs sandboxed applications and their runtimes. Application ID org.videolan.VLC identifies VLC independently of its human display name. RPM/DNF and Flatpak maintain different installed-state databases.

deeper_why.title: Remotes and scope
deeper_why.explanation: A remote is a named source such as flathub. System-wide installations and per-user installations are separate. sudo normally modifies the system installation; --user deliberately selects a user installation.

deeper_why.title: Offline limits
deeper_why.explanation: The portal has no external dependency. Adding a remote URL and downloading VLC still require operator-provided connectivity, a local mirror, cached content or an offline Flatpak bundle. Reading lessons offline does not fetch application data.

Q36.why: Runtime settings vanish unless the boot configuration reapplies them. The exercise joins both protocol families in a persistent drop-in and verifies that intended settings also reached the running kernel.

deeper_why.title: sysctl.d
deeper_why.explanation: Files ending .conf in sysctl.d provide key=value assignments loaded by system startup tooling. A dedicated /etc/sysctl.d file is easier to maintain than replacing a shared configuration wholesale.

deeper_why.title: Ordering
deeper_why.explanation: Configuration files are ordered by name and may be overridden by later assignments or other services. A high-numbered filename is a convention, not proof that nothing else overrides it. Read runtime values after applying.

deeper_why.title: Two kinds of proof
deeper_why.explanation: A file proves stored intent. sysctl output proves live state. Demonstrated reboot persistence requires an operator-controlled reboot and readback, beyond this repository-only test environment.

Q38.why: Large-file reports must contain real paths rather than permission errors or directories. The exam checks both completeness and size limits, requiring understanding of find’s predicate logic and rounded size units.

deeper_why.title: Traversal
deeper_why.explanation: find recursively walks from each starting path. / includes multiple mounted filesystems unless restricted. -type f selects regular files; directories, sockets and symlinks are different types under the default non-following behavior.

deeper_why.title: Predicate logic
deeper_why.explanation: Adjacent tests are implicitly ANDed. -size +200M selects sizes rounded up to MiB that exceed 200; -size -500M selects rounded-up MiB strictly below 500. M means 1,048,576 bytes, not decimal megabytes.

deeper_why.title: Boundary subtlety
deeper_why.explanation: The legacy grader’s expected traversal uses +200M -500M, so this lesson follows it. Because GNU find rounds up to units, -500M excludes a portion of the byte interval below exactly 500 MiB. A strict-byte variation uses c units with explicit byte thresholds; learn the distinction instead of claiming the two expressions are identical.

misconceptions.likely: The answer may treat file descriptors as interchangeable or redirections as order-independent.
misconceptions.explanation: 1 is stdout, 2 is stderr. Redirections are processed left to right; 2>&1 copies stdout’s current destination at that point.
misconceptions.micro: Shell redirection changes where each file descriptor points. In cmd >out 2>&1, stderr follows stdout into out. In cmd 2>&1 >out, stderr keeps the original stdout destination. Use separate 1> and 2> targets when the task requires separate files. Retry with harmless output in a temporary directory.
misconceptions.consequence: Diagnostics can be lost in the wrong file or mixed into a report.
misconceptions.retry: Route stdout to out.txt and stderr to err.txt.
misconceptions.man: man bash; search for “Redirections”.

misconceptions.observable: The search command is prefixed with sudo while a parent shell redirects output into a root-owned path.
misconceptions.likely: The command may assume sudo also grants permission to the shell that parses the redirection.
misconceptions.explanation: The calling shell opens redirection targets before starting the sudo command. Put the redirection inside a privileged shell when the destination requires root access.
misconceptions.micro: The shell that reads `>` opens the file. In `sudo find / ... > /root/report`, your current unprivileged shell tries to open the report before sudo starts find, so it can fail with Permission denied. Use `sudo sh -c 'find / ... > /root/report'` so the privileged shell owns the redirection, or use an appropriately privileged `tee` pipeline. The command still needs its own permissions and safe target. Retry with a harmless report under /tmp.
misconceptions.consequence: The report is not written even though the search itself is run with sudo.
misconceptions.retry: Write a harmless temporary report from a privileged shell and verify the file exists.
misconceptions.man: man bash; search for “Redirections”; man sudo.

retry_variations.prompt: In a scratch tree, find regular files strictly larger than 209715200 bytes and smaller than 524288000 bytes.
retry_variations.success: Use -size +209715200c -size -524288000c and compare near-upper-bound results to the M-unit expression.

retry_variations.prompt: Search a disposable tree while excluding traversal into mounted filesystems.
retry_variations.success: -xdev restricts traversal; explain why adding it would change this task’s all-system search scope.

retry_variations.prompt: Design a machine-consumed large-file list for paths containing newline characters.
retry_variations.success: Use -print0 and NUL-aware consumers; the original human report format assumes ordinary filenames.

capstone.prompt: Without opening the reference solution, solve the complete Q38 objective: Find large files report. Decide the host for each operation, prerequisites, required persistence, dependencies, and verification. Submit one command per line; this is a practice simulation and will not run on the VM.
capstone.objective: Large-file reports must contain real paths rather than permission errors or directories. The exam checks both completeness and size limits, requiring understanding of find’s predicate logic and rounded size units.
capstone.preconditions: Use GNU find on workstation. A full filesystem walk can be slow; the report path is root-owned and permission diagnostics are intentionally suppressed.
capstone.persistence: The report file persists at /root/large-files-report.txt; the filesystem search itself is not a scheduled job.
hints: List the objects the objective requires and choose one host for each.
Separate prerequisites, state-changing operations, persistence, and checks.
Open one command anatomy card at a time, then return to the capstone.

Q01.title: Passwordless SSH & secure file transfer
Q01.objective: Remote administration fails when authentication, hostname resolution or transfer direction is misunderstood. This lab tests key trust and exact copies between hosts, so a successful interactive login alone is insufficient.

steps.text: Create a user key on workstation. Accept a new default path only if no key exists; do not overwrite an existing private key. The isolated exercise permits an empty passphrase; production keys should be protected.
Install only the public key in student’s account on servera, authenticating with the lab-provided password.
Repeat the trust setup for the second destination.
Prove key-only login to servera. Repeat this command with serverb; a password prompt must not rescue a missing key.
Prove key-only login to serverb independently; success on servera does not establish trust on serverb.
Push the workstation file to the requested remote path.
Pull the servera account listing back to workstation.
Compare transferred bytes, not just filenames. Similarly compare ssh student@servera cat /etc/passwd against /tmp/passwd.copy.
Compare the pulled passwd file with servera’s current source bytes. No diff output and exit 0 prove equality, not merely that the file exists.

Q02.title: File & directory management
Q02.objective: Incorrect copy, move or delete choices can lose the only version of a file. The exam checks the final tree and exact contents, including paths that must disappear.

steps.text: Create all three directories without requiring the parent to exist.
Write exactly alpha followed by a newline; printf’s format is more predictable than echo’s option handling.
Create the source that will be moved.
Create the temporary third file, then remove it to practice deletion.
Copy keeps the original; mv would violate the objective.
Move and rename so file2.txt disappears.
Request confirmation before deleting only the disposable file.
Compare contents: no output and exit 0 mean the copy matches.

Q03.title: Hard links and symbolic links
Q03.objective: Links let multiple names refer to data without blindly duplicating it. The exam distinguishes a shared inode from a path pointer and may deliberately move or delete the original.

steps.text: Make a second name for the same existing inode.
Use an absolute symlink target to meet the exact path requirement.
Inspect inode numbers, link counts, modes and symlink arrow together.
Check literal target text without dereferencing the contents.

Q04.title: Directory permissions (760)
Q04.objective: Directory permissions decide whether someone can discover names, traverse paths or modify entries. Exam modes must be exact even when a deliberately unusual mode is unsuitable for normal shared-directory use.

steps.text: Apply the exact exam mode to the directory itself; avoid recursively changing every child.
Inspect the numerical mode instead of inferring it from a successful access attempt.
Read owner, group and symbolic bits for the directory itself.

Q05.title: stdout/stderr redirection
Q05.objective: Scripts must separate useful output from diagnostics or their reports become misleading. This task tests shell file descriptors and deliberately failing commands rather than the success of ls.

steps.text: Run once as student. Capture each stream independently, including the expected nonzero exit.
Read both saved files in argument order; an empty first file is acceptable.

Q06.title: grep with regex to file
Q06.objective: Account and log filtering becomes unreliable when a pattern matches too broadly. The exam checks the exact matching lines in original order, so understanding regex structure is more useful than memorizing grep text.

steps.text: Select both conditions in one regex and replace only the report file.
Review complete records and confirm ordering against the source.

Q07.title: Create gzip tar archive
Q07.objective: A backup that cannot be restored is only an assumption. The exam tests a valid gzip archive and recoverable contents, requiring awareness of both archive member paths and extraction location.

steps.text: Store relative files/... names so extraction is predictable and portable.
List stored paths without writing extracted files.

Q08.title: Extract gzip tar archive
Q08.objective: A backup that cannot be restored is only an assumption. The exam tests a valid gzip archive and recoverable contents, requiring awareness of both archive member paths and extraction location.

steps.text: Create a controlled extraction destination first.
Extract under the chosen directory; do not rely on your shell’s current path.
List stored paths without writing extracted files.
Verify the expected alpha content at its relative member path.

Q09.title: User and group management
Q09.objective: Wrong group membership either blocks work or grants unintended privilege. This exercise checks the primary group, supplementary wheel membership and password aging independently.

steps.text: Create the group before referencing it in useradd.
Assign the required primary and supplementary groups at account creation.

Q10.title: Sudoers drop-in for group
Q10.objective: A broken sudoers rule can lock administrators out or grant too much control. The exam checks group syntax, file permissions and a valid sudo configuration, not just the presence of a text file.

steps.text: Open a syntax-checking editor and enter the rule from the next command anatomy. Save only valid policy.

Keep an unprivileged account from replacing its own authorization.
Validate every included policy file before testing a new privileged session.

Q11.title: Shared directory with SGID and sticky bit
Q11.objective: Collaborative directories need both group inheritance and controlled deletion. The exam separates SGID, sticky and ordinary permissions, each solving a different problem.

steps.text: Create the collaborative directory and parent.
Set inherited group before testing new files.
Combine both special bits with full owner/group access.
Confirm group and drwxrws--T, including uppercase sticky T because other execute is absent.

Q12.objective: Package installation depends on trustworthy repository metadata, not just a URL string. This lab preserves a legacy Rocky 9 repository configuration; it is a mock configuration exercise and must not be used to replace a RHEL/Rocky 10 system’s distribution packages.

steps.text: Write the exact standalone exercise configuration, without changing other repository files.

sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/rocky.repo <<'EOF'

name=Rocky BaseOS
baseurl=https://dl.rockylinux.org/pub/rocky/9/BaseOS/x86_64/os/

gpgcheck=0
EOF

Q13.objective: Installing a command requires understanding which repository provides it and whether the package database confirms installation. The lab tests htop installation, with EPEL preparation where the configured distribution requires it.

Install the requested tool through managed packages.
Query installed state without starting the interactive tool.

Q14.title: GPT partitioning of the data disk
Q14.objective: A partitioning mistake can destroy the operating system rather than prepare extra storage. This task tests GPT layout, binary size boundaries and an LVM partition flag on the dedicated /dev/sdb lab data disk.

steps.text: Confirm size, children and mountpoints before any destructive operation. Stop if this is not the unused fixture disk.
Write a new GPT only after confirming the disk is disposable.
Create the first aligned 2-GiB partition.
steps.cmd: sudo parted -s /dev/sdb unit MiB mkpart primary 1 2049

steps.text: Mark partition 1 for LVM use.
Reserve the second aligned 512-MiB region for swap.
steps.cmd: sudo parted -s /dev/sdb unit MiB mkpart primary linux-swap 2049 2561

steps.text: Ask the running kernel to reread the table, then repeat lsblk to inspect both children.

Q15.title: LVM: PV, VG vgdata, LV lvdata
Q15.objective: LVM makes storage allocation flexible, but its layers are easy to confuse. The exam checks the PV, volume group and exact named logical volume separately.

steps.text: Confirm the fixture partition and absence of unexpected holders before PV creation.
Initialize only the intended partition as an LVM physical volume.
Create the pool and add its first PV.
Allocate a named 1-GiB LV from the group.
Verify LV name, group and allocation; pvs and vgs inspect the lower layers.

Q16.title: XFS filesystem mounted at /data
Q16.objective: Formatting and mounting are different operations: one lays out filesystem data, the other attaches it to the directory tree. The exam checks a live XFS mount, so a created directory or fstab line alone is insufficient.

steps.text: Create XFS on the confirmed empty fixture LV. Avoid -f, which would override an existing-filesystem protection.
Create the attachment directory.
Attach the filesystem now; the filesystem type can be detected from its signature.
Verify source device, target and XFS type instead of trusting an empty directory listing.

Q17.title: Swap on partition 2 with persistent fstab
Q17.objective: Swap can prevent abrupt out-of-memory failure, but a missing boot configuration leaves protection temporary. The exercise tests initialization, immediate activation and a UUID-based persistent entry independently.

steps.text: Initialize the confirmed spare swap partition from this task’s fixture.
Enable swap immediately; writing fstab alone would not activate it now.
Read the new UUID; copy the returned value into the next entry rather than guessing.
Replace the explicit placeholder with blkid’s value first. Inspect existing swap entries to avoid duplication, then append without truncating system mounts.
steps.cmd:
printf 'UUID=REPLACE_WITH_ACTUAL_UUID swap swap defaults 0 0
' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

steps.text: Validate fstab syntax and referenced sources before any reboot.
Verify active swap source and size.

Q18.title: Autofs NFS client mount
Q18.objective: An on-demand remote mount avoids blocking boot on an unavailable share, but an incorrect map leaves users with an empty directory. The exam tests path construction, the autofs service and actual access to the NFS export.

steps.text: Install the automounter from a compatible local/cached repo in an offline lab.
Inspect the master first to avoid duplicate entries, then append this mountpoint-to-map association.
Write the dedicated exercise map; its key determines the last path component.
Arrange boot activation and start the automounter now.
Access the key to trigger mounting before inspecting findmnt /nfs/share.

Q19.title: Background process with nice 15
Q19.objective: A CPU-heavy process should not compete equally with interactive work when priority can be adjusted. The exam checks the running process’s nice value, requiring correct PID selection and a clear distinction between launching and reprioritizing.

steps.text: Run on servera as student, not after a chained interactive SSH command. Launch one background process.
Immediately capture this shell’s most recent background PID, avoiding ambiguous pgrep matches.
Set the launched process’s nice value to 10.
Lower priority further; verify the result rather than assuming -n behavior.
Read the actual NI column and confirm the selected command is sha1sum.

Q20.title: User-check shell script
Q20.objective: Small administrative scripts must report truthful results without leaking diagnostic noise. The exam checks exact messages, argument handling and executable permission, so pretty-looking source alone is insufficient.

steps.text: Write literal script source; id’s status supplies the decision and both output streams are hidden.
steps.cmd:
sudo tee /root/checkuser.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
if id "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  printf 'User exists\n'
else
  printf 'User does not exist\n'
fi
EOF

steps.text: Add owner execute permission without broadening every class unnecessarily.
Test the existing-account branch through direct executable invocation.
Test the missing-account branch and exact wording.

Q21.title: Apache on 9092 with SELinux enforcing
Q21.objective: A web server can be running yet serve the wrong directory or remain unreachable. This task integrates application configuration, Unix permissions, SELinux port/content policy and service lifecycle; Q22 completes the permanent firewall setup.

steps.text: Install Apache and the package providing semanage through the operator’s compatible repository/cache.
Create the exact custom document root.
Write the required page with exact capitalization; keep it as static data.
Configure both the listener and virtual host; the old walkthrough changed only Listen and could serve the default root.
steps.cmd:
sudo tee /etc/httpd/conf.d/lab9092.conf <<'EOF'
Listen 9092
<VirtualHost *:9092>
  DocumentRoot /webdata/html
  <Directory /webdata/html>
    Require all granted
  </Directory>
</VirtualHost>
EOF

steps.text: Permit Apache to traverse/read the content directories.
Permit reading the static page without allowing ordinary users to alter it.
Permit the HTTP daemon type to bind TCP 9092. Inspect existing labels first; if already assigned, determine whether modification is appropriate.
Record a persistent labeling rule for the directory and all descendants.
Apply the stored context rule to current content.
Check configuration syntax before starting/restarting.
Enable boot startup and start now; if already active after config changes, restart after configtest.
Probe locally first. Then run Q22 and probe from servera; Q21’s grader also checks remote reachability.

Q22.title: firewalld permanent rules
Q22.objective: A service can work locally while a firewall blocks every client. The exercise tests permanent rules and their loaded runtime state, requiring the correct zone and protocol.

Store the custom HTTP port rule in the correct zone.
Also store the requested standard http service rule.

Q23.title: Default systemd target multi-user
Q23.objective: Booting the wrong systemd target can start unnecessary graphical services or omit needed capabilities. The task checks the default boot target rather than whether the current shell happens to be text-based.

steps.text: Set future boot behavior without interrupting the active session.
